RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
Loans to small and marginal farmers 
†*181.  SHRI KAPIL SIBBAL: 
SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN':†† 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of small and marginal farmers among the total 
number of farmers in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that this percentage is about 76; 
(c) whether it is a fact that small and marginal section of farmers are being 
provided only 27 per cent of total loans being disbursed for agriculture; and 
(d) if not, the annual percentage of loans extended to this section of 
farmers during the last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) As per Agricultural Census, 1990-91, the marginal and small 
holdings constituted 78.2 per cent (59.4% marginal and 18.8 per cent small), 
of the total operational holdings in the country. However, these two categories 
accounted for about 32% of the total operated area. 
(c) and (d) As per information available from the Reserve Bank of India, 
out of the total institutional credit taken for agricultural purposes from various 
sources, the small and marginal farmers were extended credit to the tune of 48.2 
per cent during 1995-96,48.7 per cent during 1996-97 and 47.25 per cent during 
1997-98, respectively.

*190. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state:

the Wild animals? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
26 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Although no specific increasing trend is discernible in the number 
of wild animals killed during last three years, there has been increased 
detection of cases of illegal hunting of tigers and leopards. 
(b) The information is being collected and will be laid on the Table of the 
House. 
(c) Hunting of all wild animals is banned under the provisions of Wild Life 
(Protection) Act 1972. The steps taken for effective implementation of the Act 
are as under— 
(1)State leve/: 
(i) State level and District level coordination committees have been set up 
in several States to prevent poaching all illegal trade in wildlife. 
(ii) State Wildlife Authorities carry out regular checking of the stock of 
dealers of animal products and birds. 
(2) National level: 
(i) Government of India has set up Regional and Sub-regional Office for 
wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country to 
prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(ii) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute wildlife 
offenders. Anti poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL. 
(iii) Financial and technical help is being extended to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant, 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-
development around Protected areas for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild 
animals. Financial assistance is, in particular, being provided for 
raising 'Strike Forces' and providing arms to the protection staff for 
combating the organised poachers. Assistance is also provided for 
giving rewards to the informers for eliciting information about poachers 
and smugglers. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
(iv) A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up 
under the chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests, 
Government of India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(v) Export of wild animals and their derivative is prohibited under EXIM 
policy. 
(vi) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching all illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(3) International level: 
(i) Government of India is a signatory to the Convention on International 
Trade in endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control 
of illegal trade in wildlife items. 
(ii) Bilateral agreements have been signed with Nepal and Republic of 
China for controlling trans-boundary illegal trade in wildlife. 
(iii) A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created for 
addressing international issues related to Tiger Conservation.

Targets of Co-operative Movement 
1034. SHRI HARE NDRA SINGH MALIK: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have achieved the targets fixed for the co-
operative movement; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, whether Government have identified the obstacles in 
achieving the targets of this movement; and 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to remove such obstacles? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b)The Government have not fixed any 
such targets for the co-operative movement. Co-operatives are organisations of 
the members i.e. shareholders. The Government, however, have been playing 
the role of a catylic agent for the promotion and development of co-operatives. 
The co-operative movement in India is the largest in the world with more than 
5,00,000 societies and about 22 crores membership covering almost 100% 
villages. The credit co- operatives advance about 43 of the total institutional 
agricultural credit. The co-operatives share in sugar production is about 56% and 
30% of the 
42 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
total fertilizer is distributed by the co-operatives. 55% of handlooms and 28% 
of the retail fare price shops are in co-operative sector. 
There has been a mixed success of the co-operatives. Some have done 
well while the others have not done so well. 
(c) and (d) Government have identified the constraints hampering 
healthy and sound development of co-operatives. These constraints are like; 
infrastructural constraints, lack of the resources, lack of professionalism, 
operational inefficiency, absence of active participation of members, 
legislative and policy constraints etc. The Government have taken certain 
steps for removing these constraints. The existing Multi-State Co-operative 
Societies Act, 1984 has been replaced by new Multi-State Co-operative 
Societies Act, 2002 to give more functional autonomy to these institutions. 
The Government has also announced a National Policy on co-operatives in 
consultation with States to provide appropriate policy and legislative 
framework to provide conducive environment for sound and healthy growth of 
the co-operative movement and to make it members driven and people's 
movement instead of Government run institutions.

Statement-I 
Details of the CSSs of the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying in 
Gujarat. 
1. National Project on Cattle and Buffalo Breeding 
The schemes of Extension Frozen Semen Technology, Progeny Testing 
Programme and National Bull Production Programme have been merged into a 
National Project on Cattle and Buffalo Breeding with higher focus on: 
• Establishment of mobile artificial insemination centres 
• Delivery of breeding inputs at farmers doorsteps 
• Strengthening of programmes for improvement of indigenous breeds 
of Cattle and Buffalo breeds. 
2. National Ram Buck Production Programme 
Under the ongoing National Ram Buck and Rabbit Breeding 
Programme, assistance is provided to the State Governments on 50:50 basis 
for the following activities: 
(i) Establishing/strengthening of state sheep, goat and rabbit breeding 
farms and  
(ii) Making market intervention operations by supporting wool boards/ 
federations. 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
3. Assistance to States for Fodder Development 
Under the centrally sponsored scheme "Assistance to States for Fodder 
Development", assistance is provided to the State Governments for the following 
activities: 
  (i) Strengthening of State Fodder Seed Farms 
(ii) Establishment of Fodder Banks 
(iii) Enrichment of straws and cellulogic waste 
(iv) Establishment of selve pasture for biomas production 
(v) Development'of Grassland and Grass reserves 
(vi) Estimation of area and production under Fodder crops. 
4. Assistance to States for Control of Livestock diseases 
The scheme of Control of Livestock diseases has the following 
components: 
(i) Systematic Control of Diseases li ke tuberculosis, Brucellosis, Swine 
Fever, Canine rabbits, Pullorum disease, Sterility, Infertility, abortions. 
(ii) Foot and Mouth Diseases. 
(iii) Animal Disease Surveillance to monitor the disease situation. 
Under the component schemes of Systematic Control of Livestock 
diseases and Animal disease surveillance, assistance is provided on 50:50 basis for 
control of livestock diseases of national importance and collection and compilation of 
information on disease situation. Under Foot and Mouth Disease Control 
Programme, assistance is provided on 25:25:50 basis to subsidise the 
vaccination against FMD, to protect high yielding cross breed and exotic cattle 
belonging to weaker section. The 50% cost of the vaccine is shared by the 
beneficiary. 
5. National Project on Rinderpest Eradication 
The OIE notified India's declaration of provisional freedom from 
rinderpest w.e.f. March 98. The project seeks to achieve "Freedom from 
Disease" and "Freedom from Infection" by March, 2002. Contingency plans to 
control outbreak of rinderpest, have also been formulated. 
48 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Assistance to States for improvement/Modernisation of Abattoirs 
and Carcass Utilisation Centres 
Under the scheme assistance as grants in aid is provided to the State 
Government to improve/upgrade the existing slaughter houses and to establish 
carcass utilisation centres. 
7. Integrated Sample Surveys for estimation of production of livestock 
products 
Under the scheme, sample surveys are conducted through the State 
Governments for estimation of production of major livestock products viz. milk, 
egg. meat and wool.The salary of the staff employed for collection of data is 
shared on 50:50 basis by the Centre and State Governments. 
8. Preservation and Development of pack animals 
Under the scheme, efforts of the St ate Governments are supplemented 
in the preservation and development of pack animals. 
9. Fishing Harbours at Major and Minor Ports 
Under the Scheme Fishing Harbours at Major and Minor Ports, 
assistance is provided to Port Trusts and State Governments for development 
of infrastructure facilities at fishing harbours and landing and berthing facilities 
for fishing crafts at minor ports. The Scheme seeks to improve the operational 
efficiency of the harbours and increase the fish production. 
10. Development of Freshwater Aquaculture 
The ongoing Scheme on Development of Freshwater Aquaculture aims 
at popularising fish farming and optimising the per hectare yield of inland fish 
resources viz. ponds, tanks and flood plain lakes.The Scheme has been 
thoroughly revised druing the current financial year by almost doubling the unit 
costs and also by incorporating new components. New components for setting 
up of freshwater prawn hatcheries, fish health diagnostic laboratories and 
integrated units including hatcheries for ornamental fisheries have also been 
included. 
11. Development of Coastal Marine Fisheries 
The Scheme of Development of Coastal Marine Fisheries seeks to 
increase production offish from coastal waters through small sector.The 
49 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
scheme has the following two components: 
(i) Motorisation of Traditional Craft 
(ii) Reimbursement of Central Excise Duty on HSD oil supplied to 
Mechanised Fishing Vessels. 
Under these components assistance is provided to fishermen for 
purchase of craft, engine and gear for mechanisation of traditional crafts and 
procurement of patrol boats. 
12. National Welfare of Fishermen 
Under the ongoing Scheme of National Welfare of Fishermen, 
assistance is provided to State Governments for providing the following 
amenities for the welfare of fishermen: 
(i) Development of Model Fishermen Village 
(ii) Insurance cover for active fishermen 
(iii) Provide financial assistance during lean season. 
13. Integrated Coastal Aquaculture 
The Scheme is implemented to exploit country's vast brackish water 
resources for shrimp cultur e. Under the Scheme, assi stance is provided to 
smallscale shrimp farmers for establishment of shrimp farms and shrimp seed 
hatcheries. Besides, assistance is given to State Governments for establishment 
of Demonstration units and training centres for providing training to shrimp 
farmers. 39 Brackishwater Farmers Development Agencies have been set up 
in the coastal States for implementation of the Scheme.

programmes by amending the State Agricultural Produce Marketing

marketing of crops (pledge financing) and to enhance their holding 
capacity to obtain remunerative price for their produce;

introducing negotiable warehousing receipt system for agricultural 
commodities; 
v. Allow future trading in all agricultural commodities to improve price 
risk management and facilitate price discovery by amending the 
Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1952; 
vi. To promote use of information technology in agricultural marketing to 
provide market led extension services to farmers and other market 
functionaries and to create facility of electronic trading to enable 
producers to directly transact business with distant buyers; and 
vii. To re-orient training and extension systems to assit farming 
community to respond to emerging challenges in agricultural 
marketing and to create an ambiance of good marketing practices in 
the country.

Unstable prices of agricultural products 
1057. SHRI HARE NDRA SINGH MALIK: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) the measures being undertaken by Government to protect farmers 
from unstable price of agricultural product;

67

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) to (f) In order to protect the farmers from 
unstable prices of agricultural products, the Government takes several measures 
which include announcement of minimum support prices (MSPs) each season of 
major agricultural commodities, undertaking price support operations of major 
agricultural commodities by the designated central nodal agencies under the 
MSP scheme and using instruments of.trade to encourage exports and 
discourage imports of agricultural commodities, etc. The designated central nodal 
agencies are r equired to intervene in the market for undertaking procurement 
operations in case the market prices fall below the MSPs fixed by the 
Government. The Government is also implementing market intervention scheme 
(MIS) for horticultural commodities and other minor agricultural crops which are 
perishable in nature.The MIS is implemented for a particular commodity on the 
request of the State Government(s) which are ready to bear 50% of the losses 
(25% in the case of north-eastern Stat es) if any, in its implementation. The 
Government has also taken various measures to promote agro export with a 
view to expand market for agricultural produce thereby helping farmers realize better 
and more stable prices. Import duties on many of the agricultural commodities have 
been increased.The imports are being closely monitored and the Government is 
determined to ensure through proper use of tariff mechanism that imports do not 
cause any injury to the domestic farmers. Fluctuation in wholesale prices of 
agricultural commodities are also monitored continuously so as to enable the 
Government to intervene in the market whenever needed.

Cutting down production cost in fertilizer units 
1068. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the so-called subsidy is being given to 
support the fertilizer units, where the cost of production is higher despite the 
fact that the higher cost of production is a result of their inefficiency, obsolete 
plant technology etc.; 
(b) whether Government are taking any steps to cut down the cost of 
production of such units; and 
(c) if so, the action Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) Urea, being the only fertilzer under 
statuory price, distribution and movement control, is covered under Retention 
Price Scheme (RPS) and is eligible for subsidy. Under RPS, the retention 
prices (cost of production plus 12% post tax return) are fixed unitwise having 
regard to a combination of various norms and actuals of various cost 
elements. Operational cost of production of urea units differs not only from unit 
to unit but also from month to month depending upon, inter alia, the health and 
vintage of the plant, the feedstock used, the levels of capacity utilization, 
specific consumption and inputs cost. Average retention price of urea 
produced by urea industry is normally higher than the maximum retail price of 
urea fixed by the Government under Essential Commodities Act. Hence, 
subsidy is given on fertilizer produced to meet the excess cost over the 
maximum retail price fixed by the Government. 
(b) and (c)The norms/parameters including consumption norms and 
plant capacity have been updated recently for the 7th and 8th Pricing Periods. 
The 7th Pricing Period will cover the period from 1.7.1997 to 
 
80

31.3.2000 whereas 8th Pricing Period will cover the period from 1.4.2000 to 
31.3.2003 or till new pricing policy comes into existence, whichever is earlier.The 
Government is also in the process of formulating a new pricing policy for urea units 
keeping in view the recommendations of Expenditure Reforms Commission for 
replacing the existing unit-specific RPS. The proposed pricing policy would be in 
the shape of Group Concession Scheme and will aim at greater transparency and 
uniformity in disbursement of subsidy payments and will induce the urea 
companies to take cost reduction measures on their own and be competitive.

1083. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDD Y: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state:

captioned, "Global Warming will hit rive, wheat yields", appearing in the Hindu 
dated 2nd May, 2002;

news-item, to counteract the adverse impact of global warming? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The impact of global warming on rice and wheat yields depends upon a 
number of factors like species and cultivar; soil properties; pests and pathogens; 
direct effect of carbon dioxide on plants;  air temperature; water stress; mineral 
nutrition; air quality and adaptive responses. The Inter Governmental Panel on 
Climate Change, which has been carrying out comprehensive assessments of 
potential impacts of climate change has projected in its Third Assessment Report 
published in 2001 that productivity of cereal crops in most cf tropical and sub-
tropical Asia may decline with increases in temperature. Degradation of soil and water 
resources, processes that are likely to be intensified by changes in temperature and 
precipitation, would be amongst major challenges for agriculture. 
(c) Various programmes and schemes of the Government including those 
relating to National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas 
(NWDPRA), Soil conservation for Enhancing Productivity   of

Cost of cleaning Yamuna in Delhi 
1089. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the 22-km stretch of Yamuna 
between Wazirabad and Okhla barrage in Delhi is only 2% of its catchment area, but 
it contributes about 80% of the river's total pollution load; 
(b) if so, what steps are being taken in this regard and what are the plans of 
the CPCB, the cost involved in the entire operation and what is the allocation 
for this financial year; and 
(c) whether any time-frame has been laid down to achieve this 
objective; if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) The 22 km stretch of Yamuna river between Wazirabad and Okhla, (which is 
less than 2% of the total catchment area) contributes on an average approximately 
310 tons/day of Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) load.This is approximately 
80% of the total pollution load reaching the river. 
(b) Under the Yamuna Action Plan (YAP) Phase-I of Government, 
pollution abatement works have been taken up in 12 towns of Haryana 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
and 8 towns of Uttar Pradesh besides Delhi. The approved cost of these works is 
Rs. 711 crore against which an expenditure of Rs. 655 crore has been incurred so 
far. The present physical progress of the works is 95%. A sewage treatment 
capacity of 750 million litres per day(mld) has been created which comprises 
322 mid in Haryana, 398 mid in Uttar Pradesh and 30 mid in Delhi. In addition, 
govt, of National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi has also taken up works of 
pollution abatement of river Yamuna in Delhi out of their own plan funds. Under 
this component, the Government of NCT of Delhi has constructed sewage 
treatment plants at 17 locations with appurtenant works.The expenditure on these 
works during the Ninth Plan was Rs. 617 crore and outlay for the year 2002-03 is 
Rs. 212 crore. The present installed capacity of sewage treatment in Delhi is 
2200 mid which also includes 30 mid capacity created under YAP Phase-I of 
Government. Apart from installation of sewage treatment plants government of 
NCT of Delhi has taken up construction of 15 numbers of common effluent 
treatment plants to address the problem of industrial pollution from 21 
industrial estates in Delhi. 
A Preliminary proposal for abatement of pollution of river Yamuna under 
YAP Phase-ll has been prepare at an estimated cost of Rs. 2018 crore. This 
proposal has been posed for funding to Japan Bank of International 
Cooperation in March, 2002. 
(c) The time frame to complete the YAP Phase-ll can be decided only 
after the project is approved. However, the Supreme Court has directed the 
Government of NCT of Delhi to ensure that the minimum desired water quality 
in Yamuna be achieved by 31st March, 2003.

Green House gases in the country;

GHG from these sectors; and 
108 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA

Abatement Strategy) Study, India's total carbon dioxide equivalent emissions for 
the base year 1990 accounted for less than 3%of the total global carbon dioxide

1095. SHRI B J. PANDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
(a) whether it is a fact that genetically modified foods are entering in our 
market from abroad; 
(b) whether the Ministry of Environment and Forests has not put any 
restrictions or curbs on import of such harmful food products; and 
(c) what safeguards have been prescribed against import of such 
harmful foods in our country? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) Rule 11 of the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage 
of Hazardous Microorganisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells 1989 
notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, provides that foods stuffs, 
ingredients in food stuffs and additives including processing aids containing or 
consisting of genetically engineered organisms or cells, shall not be produced, 
sold, imported or used except with the approval of the Genetic Engineering 
Approval Committee (GEAC). Thus, import of Genetically modified food requires 
the approval of GEAC. The GEAC considers the proposals on a case-by-case 
basis taking into account biosafety aspects including impact on human health. 
Action plan for conservation of coastal and marine Environment 
1096. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to prepare an action plan for the 
conservation of coastal and marine environment; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of achievements made by Government in this tield during 
the last ten years? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): 
(a) to (d) Ministry of Environment and Forests launched a Scheme for Conservation 
and Management of Mangroves and Coral Reefs 1986. On the recommendations 
of the National Committee on Mangroves and Coral Reefs, 30 Mangrove and 4 
Coral Reef areas in the country have 
112 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
been identified for intensive conservation and management. Management Action 
Plans for all the identified Mangrove and Coral Reef areas were prepared and 
an amount of Rs. 1317.28 lakhs was released to the State Governments/Union 
Territories concerned for implementation of these Management Action Plans 
during the Ninth Five Year Plan. As per the State of Forest Report, 1999 an 
overall increase of 615 sq. km. of mangrove areas in the country has been reported 
during the period 1991—1999.The Ministry of Environment and Forests has also 
launched an All India Coordinated Project on Coastal and Marine Biodiversity 
during'the year 1999-2000. Main activities under this project include Survey and 
Inventorisation, Training and Capacity Building in Taxonomy and Establishment of 
Database Network on the subject.The C oastal Shelterbelt Pl antation Project 
under Integrated Afforestation and Eco-Development Project Scheme envisages 
plantation in rows along the coastline to create a shelterbelt for checking soil 
erosion and sand ingress for protection of agricultural fields, homesteads and 
roads etc. To conserve and protect the fragile coastal ecosystems, Ministry of 
Environment and Forests issued Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification, 
1991 under the Environmental Protection Act, 1986. Coastal Zone Management 
Authorities have been constituted in all the coastal States/Union Territories to 
ensure implementation of the provisions  of the CRZ Notification, 1991. Coral 
Reefs have been included in Schedule 1 of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972. 
Sunderbans in West Bengal, Gulf of Mannar in Tamil Nadu and Great Nicobar 
have been designated as Biosphere Reserves. Department of Ocean 
Development has also launched a programme on Integrated Coastal and 
Marine Area Management during the Ninth Plan period.

Fake Certificate Racket 
1125. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
'Fake certificate racket busted, 3 held" published in the Asian Age dated 10th 
May, 2002; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the preventive and corrective measures to be adopted in this 
regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI RITA VERMA]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) When the reports regarding operation of certain Fake Boards 
initially came to the notice of the Central Board of Secondary Education 
(CBSE) a few years back, complaints were filed by the Board before the Police for 
taking appropriate action under the law against bogus Board called All India Board 
of Secondary Education, Delhi who had been issuing fake certificates. On 
January 27, 2000, Ministry of Human Resource Development also wrote a letter 
to the Commissioner of Police, Delhi for taking prompt action against fake Boards and 
institutions. Pursuant to the complaints filed by the CBSE and finally by the 
Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Commissioner of Police, Delhi vide 
his circular dated 4th April, 2000 has directed all the police officials that in case 
any fake educational institution has come to notice or any complaint received 
against these institutions, prompt action should be taken against them as per law. 
The names of four fake Boards including that of All India Board of Secondary 
Education have been mentioned in this circular. The Ministry of Human 
Resources Development as well as the CBSE have constituted a Malpractices 
Cell to monitor illegal activities of fake institutions and take appropriate action 
wherever required. A number of Fake Boards have been identified and publicised 
through the quarterly magazine of the CBSE and its website. Directorate of 
Education, Govt, of NCT of Delhi had also issued a Public Notice in National 
dailies on 29.1.1999 advising students and their guardians that four institutions 
including the "All India Board of Secondary Education, Delhi' are not listed 
amongst the accredited Boards and that the certificates awarded by them are not 
recognised.

Trafficking in women and children 
1126. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn towards the recent 
report of the United States, State Department, published in The Hindustan 
Times dated 10th June, 2002, under the caption, "Trafficking in women and 
children is widespread in India; 
(b) if so, what is Government's reaction on this issue; and 
(c) what steps Government propose to stop the meance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Government is concerned with the phenomena of 
intracountry trafficking of women and children and has taken the following steps to 
prevent it: 
(i)    Drawn up a National Plan of Action (1998) to Combat Trafficking and 
Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Women and Children and 
constituted a Central Advisory Committee to monitor it. 
(ii)        Set up State Advisory  Committees on Trafficking for the same 
purpose. 
(iii)     Issued guidelines to the St ates for effective implementation and 
review of the Plan of Action. 
(iv)     Initiated amendments in Immoral Trafficking (Prevention) Act to 
make it more stringent against traffickers. 
(v)   Signed SAARC Convention on combating trafficking and 
commercial sexual exploitation of women and children in January, 
2Q02. 
(vi)   Undertaken regional efforts, in aliiance with NGOs, to create 
greater awareness of the diamensions of trafficking and increase 
sensitivity tc victims among Government Departments, the police 
and judiciary, as well as within civil society at large. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
(vii) Initiated a new scheme called SWADHAR for women in difficult 
situations including victims of trafficking.The Scheme provides for 
shelter, counselling, medical assistance, vocational training to 
rescued victims. 
(viii) Formulated a model grant-in-aid scheme for.assistance to NGOs to 
combat trafficking in source areas, traditional areas and destination 
areas through prevention, resuce and rehabilitation. Emphasis is 
placed on counselling, non-formal education and vocational 
training. 
(ix) Notified officers of the level of Inspector and above in the CBI as 
Trafficking Police Officers for investigation of inter-state trafficking 
cases. 
(x) Commissioned a National Survey to go into the magnitude of the 
problem and to estimate of the numbers involved and trafficking 
routes. 
Many State Governments have also enacted legislation to prohibit 
Devdasi, Jogin and other form of sexual exploitation based on tradition. 
The National Commission for Women is conducting active advocacy against 
trafficking in partnership with NGOs. It has conducted 20 workshops all over the 
country and has prepared a comprehensive Report on the subject.

Recommendation against new railway Zones 
1131. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Railway Reforms Committee had 
suggested in 1984 the creation of very few new Zones and did not suggest 
bifurcation of Eastern Railway; 
(b) whether the Rakesh Mohan Committee has also recommended 
against creation of too many Zones; 
(c) the amount allocated for formation of the new Zone; 
(d) whether any financial cost-benefit analysis for the new Zone 
formation project has been made; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) The Railway Reforms Committee (1984) 
recommended creation of four new Zones to inter alia provide relief to the heavily 
worked existing Zones. The Committee identified the Eastern Railway as one of 
the heavily worked Zones and recommended for creation of North Central Railway, 
Allahabad, to be carved out of territorial jurisdictions of Eastern and Northern 
Railway. 
(b) The regrouping/creation of zones was neither a part of reference of the 
Committee nor part of their recommendations/executive summary. It has only 
commented upon decision of creation of new zones as an example of mixing 
policy and implementation without examining the subject in detail. 
(c) An amount of approx. Rs. 30 crore has been allocated for the year 
2002-03 for seven new Zones. 
(d) and (e) The new Zones are created by carving them out of existing Zones, 
based on the criteria of workload, accessibility, geographical sprawl and pattern of 
traffic flows and other administrative and operational requirements, so as to 
provide relief to the heavily worked Zones and improve their efficiency. 
Financial projections (in terms of additional resource generation) have neither 
been made not it is feasible to quantify them. However, even a small increase in 
efficiency is expected to give rich dividends.

profitable one

its Balance Sheet. The net loss during 1998-99,1999-2000 and 2000-01 was Rs.

(c) the Corporation has made out a Business Plan enumerating various 
steps being taken to increase their revenue. These are as follows: 
(i)     Augmentation of traffic earnings by carrying out a strong marketing 
drive. 
(ii)     Marketing its construction expertise by: 
- Trying to bid for international contracts for Railway 
construction. 
- Taking up specialised construction works such as highways and 
tunneling within the country. 
(iii) implementation the installation, after testing, of an Anti-Collision Device 
(ACD) developed by the KRC on the Indian Railway system.

Churchgate, V.T. Stations etc., who are posted at one place/post since long; and

BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Railway employees holding sensitive posts and who 
frequently come into contact with public and/or contractors/ suppliers are

railway basis. 
similarly, tenure of posting of officers working on the Zonal Railways in the 
same post should not exceed four years. No fixed tenure has been prescribed for 
stay at a particular station. 
(b) and (c) The above transfer policy is applicable to officers and 
employees working on all Zonal Railways including Jaunpur (City), Jaunpur, 
Varanasi, Mughalsarai, Alllahabad, New Delhi, Old Delhi, Nizamuddin, Kalyan, 
Mumbai Central, Churchgate, V.T. Stations, etc. Implementation of transfer

Extending National Crops Insurance Scheme to fruit bearing trees 
in Tamil Nadu 
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, Tamil Nadu is 
one of the leading mango producers in the country. Nearly six lakh metric 
tonnes of mangoes are produced in the State every year. Delicious varieties 
such as Neelum, Alphonsa, Banganapalli, Imampasand, Sendura, etc. are 
grown in various parts of Tamil Nadu. Several varieties of these mangoes are 
exported every year earning the much-needed foreign exchange. In my own 
district, Dharmapuri, different varietie s of mangoes are grown in an area of 
36,000 hectares. 
But during the last few years, the mango trees in and around 
Dharmapuri district have been attacked by insects and pests such as hoppers, 
jassids and fruit flies. Over 30 per cent of the yield has been affected by it 
resulting in heavy loss to the growers. It has also affected our export. Even 
coconut trees are affected by europhyte and other pests. Some of the pests 
attack these trees from inside and for a long time there are no symptoms of 
pest attack. The growers in this region are seriously concerned about it. The 
Tamil Nadu Government is providing assistance through the Extension 
Centres to the farmers and tree growers. But the State has limited resources. 
Therefore, I request the Central Government to extend the National 
Crop Insurance Scheme to, at least, Dharmapuri district and the surrounding 
regions in Tamil Nadu so as to cover the mango and coconut

Need to link Bagdogra Airport with more international flights for 
promoting tourism 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, there is a long-
pending demand to improve and further augment both the foreign and 
domestic passenger facilities at the Bagdogra Airport by linking it with more 
international flights. The Bagdogra Airport is not only the Gateway of North 
Bengal, it is also the gateway of the North-Eastern Region like the North-East 
Bihar and Sikkim. The three independent States Bhutan, Nepal and 
Bangladesh, are closely connected with this part of our country. This part is 
very important so far as the international tourist map is concerned.

sanctuaries, tea gardens, rich cultural heritage, great tribal traditions, the most 
beautiful Kanchanjunga Mount are all located in this region. From the high 
Sikkim Himalaya to the Bodh Gaya in Bihar, this region is famous for attracting

many other organisations are demanding that the Bagdogra Airport should be 
linked with international flights and to begin with international flights from 
Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh should be allowed to land at the Bagdogra 
Airport. If it is done, it would help to boost the economy of our country by 
augmenting foreign tourist facilities. I would request the Government of India

to this matter. Thank you.

INDEFINITE AGITATION BY NATIONAL FISHWORKERS' FORUM 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pr adesh): Sir, I want to raise 
an urgent matter of public importance. The National Fishworkers' Forum has 
decided to launch an indefinite agitation in i4^States across the country to 
press for implementation of their charter of demands. The agitation is being 
launched in Delhi, accompanied by continuous agitations in other cities like 
Mumbai, Veraval, Valsad, Panjim, Mangalore, Bangalore, 
Thiruvananathapuram, Ramanad, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Srikakulam, 
Bhubaneshwar and Contai. Most of the demands of the National Fishworkers' 
Forum pertain to the implementation of the recommendations of various 
committees appointed by the Government to study the issues raised during 
agitations in the past. These recommendations were accepted by the Central 
Government and various State Governments, but nothing has been done to 
implement them. 
Sir, the Supreme Court had passed orders regarding aquaculture in 
the Coastal Regulations Zone as far back as December, 1996. Yet, no action 
has been taken to implement these decisions. The charter of demands include 
implementation of the Murari Committee Report, adequate supply of kerosene 
for fishing at subsidized rates, stopping import of fish, implementation of the 
Mandal Commission's recommendation regarding inclusion of fishing 
community in the list of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and 
cancellation of licences to foreign vessels. It is, perhaps, a violation of the 
Indian Constitution to grant licences to foreign trawlers. Indian fishing is not a 
profession alone, it is our life-style; but, slowly, this tradition, which is a source 
of livelihood for many in our country, is being taken away. I hereby urge upon 
the Union Government to intervene in the matter and settle the demands of the 
National Fishworkers' Forum at the earliest and ensure that the right of the 
fishing community over the water bodies remains unabridged.

Development of Rail Network in Orissa 
SHRI B. J. PANDA (Orissa): Sir, my Special Mention is about the 
pressing need for developing the rail network in Orissa. The historically-famous 
Kalinga State, which is today's Orissa, has abject poverty, illiteracy and 
backwardness. Afflicted with the super cy clone in 1999, ravaged by floods last 
year, and hit by unabated drought, Orissa has remained the most neglected 
State, in the matter of development. The cash starved State has all along been 
at the mercy of the Centre or the world agencies, for development. Rich in 
minerals, the State contributes a significant 30% of the total originating 
revenue-earning traffic of the South-Eastern Railway. The State has a very 
meagre rail route length per thousand square kilometres, of only 14.0 kms., as 
against the national average of 19 kms., and the adjoining States' figures of 30 
and 43 kms. Similarly, the entire rail network is only 2340 km., in terms of route 
length. Though a number of rail-links, doublings, etc. and other projects have 
been sanctioned long ago, and the State Government has handed over land 
for construction of the rail network, the progress is quite dismal. The State 
Government has been reminding the Railway authorities for speedier 
development, but to not much avail. I would, therefore, urge upon the railway 
authorities that they should pay attention, in right earnest, complete all the on-
going projects, and take up the other sanctioned projects for immediate 
completion, to generate employment and development of this beleaguered 
area. I would also request that the next production unit should be set up in this 
State.

Need to tackle drinking water crisis in India 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, what a problem in 
India? Portends of the impending water crisis are now clearly visible in many 
parts of India. The per capita availability of water in the country has been 
reduced to less than 1000 cubic metres. It was 5000 cubic metres at the time 
of Independence, when our population was only 35 crores. In India, around 
18,365 rural habitations are not covered by any water supply programme, and 
1,53,981 rural habitations are partially covered, as per the 
214 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
2001 estimations. Rajasthan is the State where the highest number of rural 
habitations are still uncovered or partially covered by water supply schemes. 
According to experts, about 2.5 million Indians will have no access to safe 
drinking water by the year 2010. More than 50 per cent of the urban dwellers 
don't have proper water supply facilities. Slum-dwellers are the major victims 
of this menace, as water availability is very poor there. Even potable drinking 
water is not available to more than 10 per cent of the urban population. The 
existing urban water supply scheme is insufficient to meet the problem of 
water scarcity in urban areas, as these services do not cover the entire 
population. There is a need for appropriate mix of Central and State 
Governments' investment and strengthening of the operational and 
maintenance system for effective water supply. Development of technology for 
water harvesting, drought proofing measures, and production of drinking water 
is also essential. Therefore, I urge upon the Government to take innovative 
initiatives to find a permanent solution to this very important problem   -- water 
problem. Thank you, Sir.

THE INDIAN MEDICINE CENTRAL COUNCIL (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2002 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA) : Sir, I move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Indian Medicine Central Council 
Act, 1970, be taken into consideration." 
216 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, the Indian Systems of Medicine, ayurveda, unani, and siddha are 
the recognised systems of medicine in India. About 4 lakh registered 
practitioners are practising these systems in India. The system is simple, 
natural, cost-effective, and has proved to be effective for the common 
ailments as well as for chronic diseases and also for certain diseases which 
are otherwise reparatory or less amenable to other forms of treatment. 
Therefore, the Government is encouraging the system in this area to develop 
on their own genius. 
One of the measures taken to enc ourage the education and practice 
of the system is the enactment of the Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 
1970. Under the provisions of this Act, the Government, in 1971. constituted 
the Central Council of Indian Medicine, which has been reconstituted from 
time to time. The main objectives of this Council are: To maintain a Central 
Register of the practitioners of Indian medicine and to regulate the education 
and practice. Through the measures of registration of practitioners, the 
practice of Indian systems of medicine by people without any training and 
experience, has been greatly curtailed. 
Prior to the enforcement of this Act, various State Governments were 
conducting different courses of varying duration and title. In order to achieve 
standardisation and uniformity in education, the Council has enforced various 
regulations. One such regulation is the Minimum Standard .of Education in 
Indian Medicine Regulation, 1986, which was later amended in 1989. With the 
increase in acceptance and popularity of this system, the demand for 
establishing new colleges grew, resulting in an increase in the number of 
doctors coming out of these colleges. Commercialisation of medical education 
gave an incentive to the opening up of more and more colleges by societies, 
trusts and similar bodies. They started colleges, after obtaining the permission 
of the State Government and affiliati on from the universities. But the 
proliferation of colleges is leading to fall in standards. It was expected that the 
Indian Medicine Central Council Act and education regulations made by them 
would help achieve uniform standards of education and practice in ayurveda, 
unani and siddha systems of medicine. 
But, due to the lacunae in the provisions, neither the Central 
Government nor the Central Council of Indian Medicine could enforce the 
provisions in letter and spirit. According to the procedure in vogue, an 
intending society or trust can obtain the permission of the State Government 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
and the consent of the affiliating university and start a college. Thereafter, 
they approach the Central Council of Indian Medicine for permitting them to 
run the course for a fixed number of seats. There is no legal provision to make 
it obligatory on them to obtain the prior approval of the Central Government or 
the Central Council of Indian Medicine. This has led to proliferation of sub-
standard colleges. 
The Central Council of Health and Family Welfare and the 
Conference of State Health Ministers on Indian System of Homoeopathy 
addressed this issue and recommended amendment of the Indian Medicine 
Central Council Act, with a view to permitting only those colleges which 
comply with the guidelines laid down in this regard. 
Therefore, a proposal was mooted to amend the Act, on the pattern 
of the amendments carried out in the Indian Medical Council Act, in 1993. 
Similar amendments have been passed by this House in this Session, in the 
Homoeopathic Central Council Act, 1973, also. The provisions are: They have 
to seek the permission of the Central Government for the establishment of 
new colleges, increase in the number of seats, and for introducing new and 
higher courses of Indian systems of medicine, with a view to preventing the 
mushrooming of sub-standard institutions. 
Sir, with these words, I commend the Bill to the House. 
The question was proposed.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' RESOLUTION 
Crash in the prices of agricultural commodities and need for necessary steps 
to improve the conditions of farming community in the country 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN:   Shri C. Ramachandraiah to move his 
Resolution. 
SHRI C.  RAMACHANDRAIAH (ANDHRA PRADESH):    Sir,  I move 
the following Resolution:- 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
"That this House expresses grave concern over the crash in the 
prices of Agricultural commodities and the failure of the Government 
agencies toensure timely procurement with adequate minimum 
support price, throwing the millions of small and marginal famers into 
financial distress and a debt trap and urges upon the Government to 
initiate necessary steps to improve the conditions of farming 
community in the country." 
Sir, the subject is very important. Since a majority of the Members 
want to speak on the subject, I will try to finish my speech within the time 
allotted. 
The role of agriculture in the Indian economy is very vital and 
significant. Seventy per cent of the people are still depending on agriculture 
with 60 per cent of the work-force depending upon profession generally 
contributes nearly 26 per cent to the GDP. It has got a tremendous impact on 
our economy. If any particular area or a region has to be developed, it has to 
concentrate on developing the agricultural or the industrial field. Industry also 
will depend on either agricultural produce or mineral produce. Sir, the success 
or failure of the economic reforms which have been introduced in 1991 by the 
Government of India and which are being more vigorously pursued by the 
present Government, mostly depends on the success or failure of the 
agricultural sector in this country, because, still, the economy of India.is 
agrarian. But, unfortunately, the Government of India, except in the early 50s 
and 60s, has not paid that attention as should have been. Because of the 
lopsided policies and lack of comprehensiveness in the policy, agriculture was 
rather neglected, I should say. It was not protected in this country. There are 
so many distortions in the agricultural activity and I will come out with the 
reason for this deceleration. 
First, I should say that the capital formation in agriculture has been 
substantially reduced. I think, at present, it is 7.5-8 per cent of the total Plan 
Outlay that is being allocated to agriculture and its allied activities. With all its 
contribution to the national economy, it is very negligible. Sir, right from 1993-
94, the share of public investment declined. I am quoting from the figures of 
the Ministry of Agriculture. The share of public investment declined from 33 
per cent in 1993-94 to 23 per cent in 1998-99. The latest figures are not 
available with me. My information is, as on today, it is around 21.6 per cent. In 
general, only around eight per cent of the public investment in all sectors has 
gone to agriculture. 
226 
 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, it has got a cascading effect. The first effect is lesser growth of 
irrigation potentiality. Again, I will quote the figures. "The average annual 
addition to the irrigation projects from major and medium irrigation sources, 
which was about one million hectares during 1974-80, declined sharply to 0.4 
million hectares per annum during 1992-97. Of the ultimate irrigation potential 
of 139.89 million hectares, irrigation potential created is only 89.56 million 
hectares. And the total achievement up to the end of the Eighth Plan as 
percentage of the ultimate potential of major and minimum irrigation was only 
56 per cent." 
Sir, this slowdown in irrigation has affected the cropping intensity and 
yields and is a serious constraint for diversified agriculture and cropping 
patterns for productivity increases, for exports and for food security. Sir, this 
has created grave distortions in the entire agricultural sector and it has created 
a hindrance for diversification in cropping pattern which has affected the yields 
and quality also. It is widely accepted that India needs a minimum growth of 5-
5.4 per cent over a consistent period to reduce poverty significantly. At this 
growth rate, agricultural development would diversify into dairying, animal 
husbandry, pisciculture, floriculture, horticulture and other areas. This would 
spur the growth of agro-processing industries in rural areas to meet domestic 
as well as export demands. Unfortunatel y... Sir, unfortunately, we have been 
encouraging the growth of rice and wheat, that is, cereals, to the detriment of 
the nation, and to the detriment of the farmer. Rice and wheat farmers should 
be induced to look for new sources of incomes. As the world prices of wheat 
and rice are already lower than the domestic prices, and are not likely to fall, 
the domestic prices of wheat and rice will tend to fall to align with the world 
prices. Moreover, the world market for rice is very limited, and confined only to 
superfine varieties. As the demand for cereals is mainly population-driven, 
whose growth rate is slowing down, it would be prudent to divert resources 
from rice and wheat cultivation to high-value crops. 
Sir, the Government of India, over a period of time, has been 
adopting a pro-staple cereal policy, which has created these distortions. 
Today, our godowns are surplus in cereals, that is, wheat and rice, and 
disposal of the surplus has become a problem to the Government of India. We 
have been more accustomed to deal with deficits than surpluses. We find a 
problem with surpluses. Unfortunately, most of the people are still unable to 
get two square meals a day. My request is, the Government of 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
India should concentrate more on changing the cropping pattern, as per the 
needs of the ecology of the area; as per the needs of the nation. Today, we 
are importing oilseeds; we are importing pulses, and we are surplus in 
cereals, which we are unable to export, because, we are unable to compete in 
the international market. That is where the distress of the farming community 
has to be noted. 
So, another aspect of the declining capital formation in the 
agriculture is irrigation. The share of irrigation in the State expenditure has 
declined from 26.6 per cent in the Seventh Five Year Plan to 24.1 per cent in 
the Ninth Five Year Plan, whereas, allocation to research and development 
has grown from 31.7 per cent to 36.2 per cent. 
Sir, we should no doubt pay attention to rural development. But, if we 
can have introspection, the rural development always consists of very 
temporary schemes, which do not have an enduring benefit. To overcome the 
drought or famine, we have been initiating schemes under the rural 
development. Of course, in the sphere of rural development, we are spending 
more than Rs. 40,000 crores. But, it is not linked with irrigation. That is one of 
the reasons why the States have been demanding that the rural development 
funds should be given to the States directly so that the States will formulate 
their own schemes, depending upon their needs, depending upon the 
availability of local resources. The contribution of employment programmes to 
create additional employment was small, compared with * the magnitude of 
under-employment. Contribution of employment programmes, including urban 
programmes, to total employment, is about two per cent, and these 
programmes have not been integrated with agriculture, as I said earlier. The 
share of agriculture and irrigation plan expenditure has been considerbly 
reduced. It was 6.5 per cent during the Ninth Plan. So, most of the States, 
including the Government of India, have not paid much attention, and not 
allocated sufficient funds to the overall growth of irrigation in the country. Most 
of the rivers are still to be harnessed. 
Most of the potential of the rivers is still to be used, to the maximum 
advantage of the farmers. Every inch of cultivable land would be irrigated—this 
should be the policy of the Government, this should be the motto of the 
Government. The Government has to achieve that objective at any cost. 
228 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, I have spoken a number of times about the importance of 
agriculture. We have been quoting the example of China's development. For 
the past 16 years, consecutively, China ha6 been achieving a growth rate of 
more than five per cent in agriculture. In my opinion, it is only because of that 
that the economic condition of the fa rming community in China has improved. 
The farming community constitutes a large percentage of the population even 
in China. The higher growth rate in agriculture has improved their economic 
condition and has enabled them to purchase more goods. That has increased 
the aggregate demand for their goods and pushed up the economy. 
Unfortunately, here, the policy-framers have not been heeding to the request 
of the farmers because they have been adopting a lop-sided policy in 
planning. So, this is the state of affairs prevailing today. It is only because of 
the lop-sided policy of the Government. 
Sir, if we come to the agricultural credit rate, till today, we have left 
the farming community to the vagaries of the monsoon. We are forcing them 
to pray to God for timely monsoon so that they can irrigate their land with rain 
water. There is no security mechanism built, over a period of time, in this 
country for the betterment of the farming community. In 1998-1999, the 
agricultural credit rate was 6.2 per cent; in 1999-2000, it was 1.3 per cent; and 
in 2000-2001, it was minus .2 per cent. Unless the credit rate is increased, it 
will be very difficult to improve the economic standards of the majority of the 
people. Sir, I want to point out one of the reasons why the deceleration has 
taken place. The contribution of agriculture to the GDP is 25-26 per cent. The 
exposure to agricultural credit rate is very minimum. It is somewhere between 
14 and T6 per cent, in the morning, the Minister of Agriculture has mentioned 
in reply to a question that the small and marginal farmers constitute 78.5 per 
cent, and their operated area is only 32 per cent. Very good! The Government 
seems to be satisfied because the operated area is only 32 per cent. They are 
providing 48 per cent of the total agricultural credit to the small and marginal 
farmers. The Government is aware that most of the farmers who have got big 
holdings may not require agricultural credit, because they are self-sufficient 
and have got enough resources to undertake the activity. It is the small and 
marginal farmers who need the credit more. So, the Government should 
increase not only the percentage of total agricultural credit, but also the 
percentage of agricultural credit to the small and marginal farmers. 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
Sir, I want to mention one thing more --the rate of interest. I will give 
you the data about other countries. In USA, the contribution of agriculture to 
the GDP is two per cent, and the labou r-force is four per cent. They are 
charging four per cent for agricultural cr edit. In France, their contribution to the 
GDP is two per cent, and the labour- force is six per cent. They are charging 
four per cent. In Germany, their contribution is one per cent, and the labour-
force is three per cent. The interest rate is also three per cent. In England, their 
contribution to the GDP is two per cent, and the labour-force is three per cent. 
They are charging an interest rate of five per cent. In India, their contribution is 
26 per cent, and the labour-force is 60-70  per cent. But we are charging a 14 
per cent rate of interest from the farming community! So, with all these 
distortions, how does the Government think that the agricultural growth will be 
more viable? 
Another aspect is that, the small and marginal farmers have no 
access to institutional finance. No institutional credit is available to the small 
and marginal farmers. They take land on lease from landholders. They can't 
raise loans because they are not the owners of the land. Unless you own the 
land, you will not be eligible to get loans. What I am suggesting is, let us have 
crop tenancy, instead of land tenancy. The land-owners will not permit the 
lessees to raise loans because it will crea te some interests or something. They 
have got their own apprehensions. My request is, let us have crop tenancy so 
that the small and marginal farmers will have access to institutional credit. 
There is another aspect which relates to the minimum support price. It 
has got two angles. It never depends on t he cost of raising the crops. If you 
consider the MSP of differen t crops for the past four or five years, you will find 
that it has been arbitrarily fixed. There has been an arbitrary increase of Rs.15 
or Rs.20 per quintal every year. It was in no way related to the cost of 
production. But the interest rates were fixed, entirely to the detriment of the 
farming community. 
Another point-it is subject to correction-is that, 10 per cent of the 
procurement price is being paid to the St ate Governments. That is what I was 
told. When the FCI procures an item at Rs. 1,000 per quintal, an amount of 
Rs.100 is being paid to the State Governments, by way of one per cent market 
tax, four per cent sales-tax and five per cent rural development cess.   I have 
got a doubt whether we are providing subsidy to 
230 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the farmers or the farmers are subsidising the Government through their 
activities. I feel, it is not the agricultural activity which is helping the farmers to 
survive. It is the other supplemental income that the farmers get, which helps 
them to survive. The agricultural work will keep the small and marginal farmers 
engaged and, at the most, they will get what they spend. They will never make 
any profit out of the agricultural activities . This is the state of affairs prevailing 
in the country. There is one more aspect to the minimum support price. As I 
have stated, access to institutional credit is not available to the small and 
marginal farmers. They are, virtually, driven to the conventional money-
lenders. Before they start raising the crops, the farmers take loans from 
conventional money-lenders, with a commitment that they will give the crop to 
them. Therefore, whatever the minimum support price that the Government 
fixes, has no relevance to the small and marginal farmers, who have already 
made a commitment to the moneylenders.  Since no access to institutional 
credit is available to the small and marginal farmers, they are driven to the 
conventional money-lenders. In case there is a crop failure, and he is unable 
to redeem the debt, it will force him to commit suicide. The Government has to 
consider long-term and short-term meas ures, because the agricultural assets, 
which the Government creates, confer some enduring benefits on the major 
section of the population; rather than spending on rural development. I don't 
say that you allocate a small amount for R & D .  RuraJ development has to be 
encouraged. But the benefits derived by the community out of rural 
development are temporary. The assets that are being created in the 
agricultural and irrigation fields, should be used for the benefit of the farming 
community. It has to be balanced. It should be seen where exactly the society 
needs agricultural development and rural development. 
Today we are spending lakhs of rupees on four-laning roads and Six-
laning roads. \ do not say that you should not do it. But, can we afford to do it 
with the very meagre resources that are available at the disposal of the 
Government? They money has to be spent very judiciously. When the villages 
are languishing without roads, when there is no production in factories to 
transport goods because of the deceleration or slowing down of the economy, 
when a major section of the population does not have money to mobilise 
resources, I think that is a luxury to day. It may be a necessity tomorrow. You 
should spend that amount in creating more assets and irrigation projects; link 
all the rivers in this country; provide water to every inch of the land.   It would 
create more employment and more wealth in the 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
3.00 p.m. 
country and people would have the purchasing capacity to acquire goods. It 
would boost the economy. We don't need any graduates from the London 
School of Economics or the Harvard University to propagate all these things.   
It is a question of prudence. 
Sir, there are hundreds of works which are still pending at the village 
level. I am not against big dams. These days there is a lot of controversy about 
the big dams in our country. If it is a big project, there comes the question of 
cost overrun and time overrun. If you go in for small projects in villages, you 
can derive more benefits, like soil conservation, water harvesting, as we have 
been doing in Andhra Pradesh. These small projects can be completed in a 
short span of time and people can derive benefit immediately. 
Whatever minimum support price the Government may offer, unless 
the productivity is increased, there is no use of it. Today, the average wheat 
production in our country is 2.4 to 2.7 metric tonnes per hectare; whereas, in 
other countries it is 7 metric tonnes per hectare. Even if you increase the 
minimum support price, you cannot atta in the level of 7 metric tonnes per 
hectare. If you fix a price of Rs. 1,00 0 per metric tonne, you would get Rs. 
2,700/-; whereas, the other countries would get Rs. 7,000 per metric tonne. 
The Government has to ponder over this issue. Efforts should be made to 
increase the productivity in this country. 
Sir, our product is not competitive because we are unable to achieve 
the productivity and we are unable to maintain the quality in order to compete 
in the international market. Every country in the world has got an objective to 
address to the global needs. Our exposure in the world market in terms of 
export of agriculture produce is to the extent of 0.6 per cent wnich is very 
negligible and invisible. It is nowhere visible in the international market. Why is 
it happening? It is happening because you have neglected the agriculture 
sector from the beginning. You want to create superficial development which is 
not going to yield results. 
That is not yielding result. So, or ientation towards exports has to be 
done. Produce those which can be exported; change the cropping pattern so 
that the farmers get the maximum benefit. 
232 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, one more thing which the Government has to focus its attention 
on, is with regard to crop insurance. Of course, we have the crop insurance 
scheme. But, in our area, the people say, it is not crop insurance but it is a 
loan insurance. If somebody borrows loan on a crop, insurance is there, but it 
is to cover the loan and not the crop. So, do we call it crop insurance or loan 
insurance? Our demand is, create a separate corporation run by 
professionals, -- not by IAS officers who do not have any knowledge about 
agriculture in this country, -- extend this activity to all the crops and to all the 
areas of the country. Then, as regards the farming subsidy, to what extent are 
we protecting the farming community in this country? We say that we are 
providing subsidies to them. Is it really so? When we are unable to provide 
them even the cost of production, ho w can we claim that we are providing 
subsidy to the farmers, whereas they are providing revenue to the 
Government, in terms of sales tax, transportation costs, etc. Sir, the 
agricultural health of this country should not be neglected on any account. 
Sir, one more thing is, we have agricultural experts running the 
Ministry of Agriculture; we have experts in every activity of the Ministry, but 
persons who do not have basic knowledge about agriculture are being kept at 
the helm of affairs. And, it is becoming very difficult to give feedback to the 
Government so that they can take good decisions". Till now, the Government, 
whichever party had been in power, has been advised not to adopt a pro-
staple cereal policy, and this has caused total detriment to the country. Today, 
we are importing oilseeds, pulses, etc., and we are spending thousands of 
crores on foreign exchange. This is because of the lopsided policies of the 
Government, which will have to be rectified.      . 
Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity and I request the 
Government to initiate all these measures so that the agricultural activity, 
which is the lifeline of our country, can flourish.  Thank you.

SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Sir, I congratulate my 
hon. colleague for raising a very important issue in our country. I am in full 
agreement with the concern expressed in the Resolution. I join with him in 
urging upon the Government to take all appropriate measures to protect the 
interests of the agricultural workers, the peasants and the common people in 
this country. It is a fact that the prices of most of the agricultural commodities 
have crashed. The price of coconut, the price of arecanut, tobacco, and, 
recently, the price of raw silk, have all crashed. I do not want to extend the list.    
The prices of almost all crops have crashed. 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2002] 
Because of the price crash, the peas ants are suffering, the agricultural 
workers are suffering, the common people are suffering, and the economies of 
most of the States are facing great difficulties because of the crash in the price 
of most of these agricultural commodities. How to deal with this most important 
issue? To me, there should be a two-pronged approach to tackle the problem. 
One is, certain immediate measures, to protect the interests of the peasants, 
the agricultural workers, and the common man, should be taken. Secondly, 
there should be, a re-look, a re-thinking, into the whole gamut of the basic 
policies which we are pursuing in the agricultural sector, particularly, in the 
context of the WTO regime. Sir, the mover of the Resolution has already 
brought to our notice - yes; the investments are not picking up, and there is a 
drastic fall in the public investments. The capital formation is facing serious 
problems. So, what is in store for us? If investment does not pick up, if capital 
formation does not pick up, the future is very bleak, and if you look at the 
productivity increase with regard to most of the crops, you will find that it is 
stagnant, and, as far as foodgrains production is concerned, during the last 
decade, the rate of growth has come down below the rate of growth of 
population. 
So, to me it looks, if the present situation continues like this, our 
country would be sliding towards foodgrains shortage and starvation deaths. 
Of course, the contradiction is that, even in such a situation, we have a record 
foodgrains stock, to the tune of 65 million tonnes. I am not going into all these 
details because I do not have enough time at my disoposal to go into them. It 
is because of the decline in the purchasing capacity of the people and due to 
various other reasons that are there. All these indicators show that our future 
is very bleak. 
Now, how to approach this issue? According to me, the mover of tbe 
Resolution has mainly drawn our attention to the crash in the prices of 
agricultural commodities. But this time there is a qualitative change in the 
overall situation. Earlier also prices have fallen, but the earlier phenomena 
were one of price fluctuations. Now, some sort of a permanent price crash has 
set into the system. Earlier, at the ti me of the harvesting season, the traders 
and industrialists, who purchase these crops, disappeared from the market 
and the poor, who did not have enough resources, were forced to sell at 
cheap rates. After the harvesting season was over, the traders and 
industrialists would come in. Such fluctuations were there in earlier times. And 
in the case of certain crops, which have a potentional for export, 
244 

[26 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
because there is no demand in the external  market, there is a chance of a fall 
price. Similarly, in the case of certain crops, which can be imported from other 
countries, if there is a surplus in the world market, there is a chance of a fall in 
price. Such fluctuations were there in existence during the last so many years. 
We took certain interim measures to prot ect the interests of the agriculturists, 
the workers and the common man. Now, after the WTO regime has come into 
existence, this has become some sort of a permanent thing. The prices of 
most of the crops have fallen and they are not picking up. Why has this 
qualitative change come about in the prices of these crops? The IMF, the 
World Bank and the WTO, are giving instructions to us. They are asking us to 
remove all quantitative restrictions. Earlier, there was a protected market. 
Because India was a backward country, we wanted protection in order to 
develop our economy. We have the past of a century-long colonial 
exploitation. Such countries do require protected markets. Such countries to 
require Government intervention. Now, because of the new regime, there is no 
restriction either on imports or exports. There is every possibility of a world 
market slowly emerging, and the price fluctuations that we face in the 
international market are also experienced in our domestic market. Because of 
the instructions from the international bodies, our Government has more or 
less withdrawn from many fields. It has retreated from many areas, and there 
is an operation of free market forces. The Government has withdrawn from the 
field of irrigation and power, science and technology and infrastructure! 
facilities. The Government has also reduced the subsidies on almost all the 
inputs. Because of all these things, the peasants are facing problems. 
Not only that. The mover of the Resolution has asked for the 
provision of a Minimum Support Price and intervention of the Government. I 
am asking him: If the present Government is pursuing the present policies, 
would it be possible for the Government to intervene in the market? Would it 
be possible for the Government to provide a Minimum Support Price? Sir, 
already, we are discussing a Competition Bill. That was discussed in the WTO. 
The international body decided, "Yes, we will continue the discussion." But, 
our Government is coming forward with a Competition Bill. And, what is the 
essence of the Competition Bill? The Government withdraws. If the 
Government actually declares a Minimum Support Price and intervenes in the 
market, as per the present provisions of  this Bill, it will be an abuse of 
competition, it may be punishable. So, withdrawal of the Government. ...(Time-
bell).
